content: Spermicides are chemical agents designed to kill sperm, and they are inserted into the vagina before sexual intercourse to prevent pregnancy. While spermicides can be used as a standalone contraceptive method, their effectiveness is lower compared to other contraceptive options. For this reason, spermicides are often used in combination with barrier methods such as diaphragms, condoms, cervical caps, or contraceptive sponges. This combined approach is believed to reduce the likelihood of pregnancy more effectively than using either method alone. Modern spermicides are typically unscented, clear, unflavored, non-staining, and provide lubrication. Types and Effectiveness The most commonly used active ingredient in spermicides is nonoxynol-9, which is available in various forms, including gels, films, and foams. When used correctly and consistently, spermicides have a failure rate of approximately 18% per year, but this increases to 29% with typical use. Another spermicide, menfegol, is available in Europe as a foaming tablet. Octoxynol-9, once a common spermicide, was removed from the U.S. market in 2002 due to a lack of updated studies required by the FDA. Other spermicidal agents, such as benzalkonium chloride and sodium cholate, are used in some contraceptive sponges, and benzalkonium chloride may also be available in Canada as a suppository. There are several myths surrounding unconventional substances as spermicides. For example, the idea that Coca-Cola or other soft drinks can act as effective spermicides is entirely false. Laboratory studies have shown that lemon juice solutions and certain beverages like Krest Bitter Lemon can immobilize sperm, but their use as a postcoital douche is unlikely to be effective because sperm begin leaving the ejaculate and entering the cervical canal within 1.5 minutes of ejaculation. Furthermore, no published studies have confirmed the effectiveness of lemon juice preparations in preventing pregnancy. Lactic acid-based spermicides have shown some spermicidal effects, and commercial products are available, but no significant research on their contraceptive efficacy has been conducted since 1936. Neem plant extracts, such as neem oil, have demonstrated contraceptive effects in laboratory and animal studies, but human trials to confirm their effectiveness in preventing pregnancy have not yet been conducted. Use as Microbicides Spermicides have also been investigated for their potential use as microbicides to prevent sexually transmitted infections (STIs), including HIV. VivaGel is the only sexual lubricant that has shown effectiveness as a microbicide against HIV and herpes in animal studies, and it is undergoing further clinical trials in Australia and the United States. Nonoxynol-9 was previously thought to reduce the risk of HIV transmission because it inhibits the virus in laboratory settings. However, human studies have shown that nonoxynol-9 does not provide protection against HIV and may even increase the risk of transmission. This is because frequent use of nonoxynol-9 can cause abrasions in the vaginal and rectal walls, which facilitate the entry of pathogens. Similarly, while lemon juice has been proposed as a microbicide, the concentrations required to kill HIV also cause tissue damage, making it unsuitable for this purpose. Neem extracts have also been studied for their antimicrobial properties, but Phase I clinical trials revealed that nearly half of participants experienced side effects such as genital itching, burning, and pain. Although no serious adverse effects were reported, further trials to assess efficacy (Phase II) have not yet been completed. Use with Condoms Some condoms are pre-lubricated with nonoxynol-9 by manufacturers. However, according to Consumer Reports, spermicidally lubricated condoms do not offer additional protection against pregnancy compared to regular condoms. They also have a shorter shelf life and may increase the risk of urinary tract infections in women. The World Health Organization (WHO) has recommended against promoting spermicidally lubricated condoms but advises that they are still preferable to using no condom at all. In contrast, applying a separately packaged spermicide alongside condom use is believed to enhance contraceptive efficacy. Side Effects Nonoxynol-9 can cause side effects, including irritation, itching, or burning of the genital area in either partner. In women, it may also lead to urinary tract infections, yeast infections, or bacterial vaginosis. These side effects are relatively uncommon, with studies indicating that only 3-5% of women discontinue spermicide use due to adverse effects. Concerns have been raised about the potential for birth defects in children conceived despite spermicide use or in cases where women unknowingly continued using spermicides during early pregnancy. However, a 1990 review of large studies concluded that there is no increased risk of congenital anomalies, altered sex ratios, or early pregnancy loss among spermicide users. Historical Use The earliest documented use of spermicides dates back to the Kahun Papyrus, an Egyptian text from 1850 BCE, which described a pessary made from crocodile dung and fermented dough. The acidic nature of the dung likely had a spermicidal effect. The Ebers Papyrus, dating to approximately 1500 BCE, recommended a mixture of seed wool, acacia, dates, and honey, which was inserted into the vagina. This formulation likely worked as both a physical barrier and a chemical spermicide due to the lactic acid produced by the acacia. In the 2nd century CE, the Greek physician Soranus described several acidic mixtures for spermicidal use, which were applied by soaking wool and placing it near the cervix. Modern research into spermicides began in the 19th century, focusing on substances that could inhibit sperm motility. Nonoxynol-9 and menfegol were developed as a result of this research. However, many ineffective substances were also marketed, particularly after the 1873 Comstock Act in the U.S. made contraception illegal. During this time, spermicides were often sold as feminine hygiene products without any standards for effectiveness. Some products, such as Lysol, were even marketed for use as postcoital douches, which were too late to prevent sperm from reaching the cervix. Medical estimates from the 1930s suggested that the pregnancy rate for women using over-the-counter spermicides was as high as 70% per year.
